questions.q: The force between two point charges varies as:
questions.solution:
$F = \dfrac{Q_{1}Q_{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}r^{2}}$ — an **inverse square** law, exactly like gravity.

The field lines spread over a sphere whose area grows as $r^{2}$, which is the geometric reason behind both.

questions.q: Electric field strength is defined as:
questions.solution:
$E = \dfrac{F}{Q}$ — **force per unit positive charge**, in N/C or V/m.

$\dfrac{W}{Q}$ is the **potential**, a scalar. Field is a vector; potential is not.

questions.q: The gravitational field strength at the surface of a planet of mass $M$ and radius $R$ is:
questions.solution:
$g = \mathbf{\dfrac{GM}{R^{2}}}$.

It is the same $g$ that appears in $W = mg$ — the field strength and the acceleration of free fall are the same quantity.

questions.q: The gravitational potential at infinity is taken to be:
questions.solution:
Zero at infinity, so all gravitational potentials are **negative**: $V = -\dfrac{GM}{r}$.

The negative sign means work must be **done** to escape, and it is what makes escape velocity a finite, calculable quantity.

questions.q: The field between two parallel plates a distance $d$ apart at potential difference $V$ is:
questions.solution:
$E = \dfrac{V}{d}$, uniform between the plates and directed from positive to negative.

This is why field strength can be quoted in V/m as readily as in N/C — the two units are identical.

questions.q: Find the force (in N) between charges of $2\,\mu$C and $3\,\mu$C, $0.1$ m apart. Take $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}} = 9 \times 10^{9}$.
Find the field strength (in V/m) between plates $2$ mm apart with a potential difference of $500$ V.
Find $g$ (in m/s$^{2}$) at the surface of a planet with $\dfrac{GM}{R^{2}} = 3.7$ SI units.
questions.solution: $g = \mathbf{3.7}$ m/s$^{2}$ — about the value on Mars, roughly $38\%$ of Earth's.

questions.q: Find the force (in N) on a charge of $4\,\mu$C in a field of $2 \times 10^{5}$ V/m.
A satellite orbits at radius $r$ where $\dfrac{4\pi^{2}r^{3}}{GM} = 7.2 \times 10^{7}$ s$^{2}$. Find its period, in hours, correct to one decimal place.
questions.solution:
$T = \sqrt{7.2 \times 10^{7}} = 8485$ s $= \mathbf{2.4}$ hours.

This is Kepler's third law, $T^{2} \propto r^{3}$, in the form that follows from Newton's law of gravitation.

questions.q: Compare gravitational and electric fields, listing their similarities and their differences.
questions.solution:
**Similarities.**

1. Both are **inverse square** laws: $F = \dfrac{GMm}{r^{2}}$ and $F = \dfrac{Q_{1}Q_{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}r^{2}}$.

2. Both define **field strength** as force per unit mass or charge.

3. Both have a **potential** defined as energy per unit mass or charge, with zero taken at infinity.

4. Both have field strength as the **negative gradient of potential**: $g = -\dfrac{dV}{dr}$.

5. For both, potential $\propto \dfrac1r$ while field $\propto \dfrac{1}{r^{2}}$.

**Differences.**

1. **Gravity is always attractive**; electric forces may attract or repel, because charge comes in two signs and mass in only one.

2. **Electric fields can be shielded** — a Faraday cage excludes them entirely. Gravity cannot be screened by anything.

3. **Electric forces depend on the medium** (through $\varepsilon_{r}$); gravity does not.

4. **Gravity is astonishingly weaker.** Between two protons the electrostatic repulsion exceeds the gravitational attraction by a factor of about $10^{36}$.

**Why gravity dominates the universe despite being so weak.** Charges cancel: bulk matter is almost exactly neutral, so electric forces cancel over large distances. Mass never cancels, so gravity accumulates — and at astronomical scales it is the only force left standing.

questions.q: Derive the relation between orbital period and radius for a satellite, and explain what makes an orbit geostationary.
questions.solution:
**Derivation.** Gravity supplies the centripetal force:

$\dfrac{GMm}{r^{2}} = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}$

$v^{2} = \dfrac{GM}{r}$

For a circular orbit, $v = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T}$:

$\dfrac{4\pi^{2}r^{2}}{T^{2}} = \dfrac{GM}{r}$

$\mathbf{T^{2} = \dfrac{4\pi^{2}r^{3}}{GM}}$

So $T^{2} \propto r^{3}$ — **Kepler's third law**, derived rather than merely observed.

**Note the satellite's mass cancels**: every satellite at a given radius has the same speed and period, whatever its size.

**A geostationary orbit** requires three conditions:

1. **Period exactly $24$ hours**, matching the Earth's rotation.

2. **Directly above the equator** — any other orbit would carry the satellite north and south each day.

3. **Moving west to east**, in the direction of the Earth's spin.

Putting $T = 86\,400$ s into the formula gives $r \approx 42\,000$ km from the Earth's centre, or about $36\,000$ km above the surface.

**Why it matters.** Such a satellite hangs permanently over one point, so a receiving dish can be bolted in place and never moved. It is how satellite television and much intercontinental communication works — and it is why every such dish in a country points the same way.

questions.q: Define electric potential, explain why it is negative for gravity but may be either sign for electric fields, and calculate the escape velocity from a planet.
questions.solution:
**Electric potential** at a point is the **work done per unit positive charge** in bringing a small test charge from infinity to that point.

$V = \dfrac{W}{Q}$, in volts. It is a **scalar**, which makes it much easier to combine than field strength — potentials from several charges simply add algebraically.

**Why gravitational potential is always negative.** Gravity is always attractive, so a mass brought in from infinity **gains** kinetic energy and its potential energy falls below the zero taken at infinity.

$V = -\dfrac{GM}{r}$ — negative everywhere, approaching zero only at infinity.

**Why electric potential may be either sign.** Near a **positive** charge, work must be done **against** repulsion to bring a positive test charge in, so $V$ is positive. Near a **negative** charge the test charge is attracted, so $V$ is negative.

**Escape velocity.** An object escapes if its kinetic energy is at least equal to the depth of the potential well:

$\tfrac12 mv^{2} = \dfrac{GMm}{R}$

$\mathbf{v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}} = \sqrt{2gR}}$

**For Earth:** $v = \sqrt{2 \times 9.81 \times 6.4 \times 10^{6}} = 11.2$ km/s.

**Two things to notice.** The escaping object's **mass cancels** — a pebble and a spacecraft need the same speed. And the escape velocity does not depend on direction, only on speed, since energy is a scalar.

**Why the Moon has no atmosphere:** its escape velocity is only $2.4$ km/s, which the faster gas molecules exceed, so over billions of years the atmosphere has leaked away.

questions.q: Describe the field lines and equipotential surfaces for an isolated point charge and for two parallel plates, and state the relation between them.
questions.solution:
**Isolated point charge.**

• **Field lines:** straight lines radiating outward from a positive charge, inward to a negative one. They crowd together near the charge, where the field is strongest.

• **Equipotentials:** concentric **spheres** centred on the charge. They are drawn at equal intervals of potential, so they get **further apart** as you move away — potential changes more slowly where the field is weaker.

**Parallel plates.**

• **Field lines:** straight, parallel and evenly spaced, running from the positive to the negative plate — a **uniform** field, except for slight bulging at the edges.

• **Equipotentials:** flat planes parallel to the plates, **evenly spaced** because the field is uniform.

**The relation between them.**

1. Field lines are always **perpendicular** to equipotential surfaces.

2. $E = -\dfrac{dV}{dx}$ — the field is the **negative potential gradient**, pointing the way potential falls fastest.

3. **No work is done** moving a charge along an equipotential, since $\Delta V = 0$.

**Why perpendicular.** If the field had any component along an equipotential, work would be done in moving along it — contradicting the definition. So nothing is left but the perpendicular component.

**The map analogy:** contour lines are equipotentials and water runs at right angles to them, straight down the steepest slope. Closely spaced contours mean a steep hillside — and closely spaced equipotentials mean a strong field.

questions.q: Describe the path of a charged particle entering a uniform electric field perpendicular to the field lines, and compare it with a projectile in a gravitational field.
questions.solution:
**The two components.**

**Along the original direction:** no force, so the velocity is **constant**: $x = vt$.

**Along the field:** a constant force $F = EQ$, so a constant acceleration $a = \dfrac{EQ}{m}$, and $y = \tfrac12 at^{2}$.

**Eliminating $t$:**

$y = \dfrac{EQ}{2mv^{2}}x^{2}$

— a **parabola**, exactly as for a projectile under gravity.

**The comparison.**

• Both have constant velocity in one direction and constant acceleration perpendicular to it.

• Both give parabolic paths.

• **But gravity accelerates every mass equally** ($a = g$, independent of $m$), while an electric field accelerates particles according to their **charge-to-mass ratio** $\dfrac{Q}{m}$.

**That difference is what makes the technique useful.** Particles of different $\dfrac{Q}{m}$ deflect by different amounts and can be separated and identified.

**Where it is used.** J. J. Thomson measured the electron's charge-to-mass ratio exactly this way, and so discovered the electron. The same principle deflects the beam in an oscilloscope, sorts ions in a mass spectrometer, and steers the droplets in an inkjet printer.

**A magnetic field behaves quite differently:** its force is perpendicular to the velocity, so it curves the path into a **circle** rather than a parabola, and does no work at all.
